title: Finding the Y-Intercept: Why x Must Be Zero

scenes.title: Where does 2x + 3y = 12 cross the y-axis?
body: We want the y-intercept, not just a random point on the line.
The key question is: what must x equal on the y-axis?
scenes.narration: Find the y-intercept of two x plus three y equals twelve. Here’s the idea: an intercept is not a formula trick. It is a location on the graph. The y-intercept is where the line actually touches the y-axis, so before doing any algebra, ask what is always true about every point on that axis.

scenes.title: On the y-axis, x is always zero
body: Every point on the y-axis has the form (0, y).
Common mix-up: setting y = 0 finds the x-intercept instead.
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. To find a y-intercept, set x equal to zero, because every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate zero. If you set y equal to zero, you are finding where the line hits the x-axis. So the variable you set to zero is the coordinate that vanishes on the axis you are crossing.

scenes.title: Substitute x = 0 and solve
scenes.narration: Now the algebra follows the geometry. Substitute x equals zero into the equation. Two times zero disappears, leaving three y equals twelve. Divide by three and y equals four. That means when the graph is on the y-axis, its y-coordinate is four.

scenes.title: Why this matches y = mx + b
body: The constant 4 is b because x = 0 makes the slope term disappear.
scenes.narration: Notice why the same answer appears in slope-intercept form. If we rewrite the equation, we get y equals negative two thirds x plus four. In y equals m x plus b, b is the y-intercept because when x is zero, the m x term becomes zero and only b remains. So b is not a memorized label; it is the output when x equals zero.

scenes.title: Write the intercept as the point (0, 4)
scenes.narration: The y-intercept is the point zero, four, not just the number four when the question asks for a point. Check it in the original equation: two times zero plus three times four equals twelve, so the point lies on the line. The main idea is simple: the y-intercept is the output when x equals zero.
